posts.author: Lakshay Singhal
posts.headline: Senior Software Development Engineer at Be10x
posts.text: Everyone is saying software engineering is finished. But one perspective from a Google Engineering Manager with nearly 20 years in tech suggests that what’s really changing is the role of the engineer—not the need for engineers. AI isn't replacing software engineers overnight. It is changing what engineers need to be good at. 1. Coding is changing, not disappearing The value is shifting toward problem-solving, architecture, edge cases, and understanding the customer. 2. We're entering the agentic era AI can now handle increasingly complex tasks, but giving it a completely new real-world problem and expecting it to independently understand context and own the outcome is still a much higher bar. 3. Fresher hiring will get harder "I know Java + LeetCode" won't be enough. Engineers will need to show they can build with AI, question its output, and take ownership of what ships. 4. CS fundamentals still matter Focus on: → DSA → OS & Networks → Distributed Systems → System Design → Problem Solving 5. Interviews will evolve Expect more questions like: → Debug AI-generated code → Find security issues → Scale a system → Review an AI solution The question shifts from "Can you write code?" to "Can you judge code?" 6. Teams won't necessarily shrink dramatically The same team may simply become far more productive, with more emphasis on senior-level thinking and decision-making. 7. Human value moves toward judgment Business context. Trade-offs. Collaboration. Ownership. When production breaks, someone still needs to understand the problem and own the fix. 8. Learn fundamentals before relying on AI Code without AI first. Understand how systems work. Then use AI aggressively—as a partner, not a replacement for understanding. 9. If you learn only 3 things this year: → Agentic workflows → Systems + data architecture → Business understanding The future of software engineering may not be about writing less code. It may be about thinking better about the code AI helps you write. posts.author: Hasnat Awan, AMIMechE
posts.headline: Graduate Mechanical Engineer at Southern Water
posts.text: Graduate jobs aren’t simply “disappearing because of AI” — but the skills employers expect from graduates are changing fast. A UK government analysis published this year found that overall UK hiring was 14% lower year-on-year in April 2026. Among the entry-level occupations it tracked, Accountant roles were down 29% and Software Engineer roles were down 27%. In total, 30 of the 38 entry-level occupations analysed had seen hiring decline. That sounds worrying — especially if you are graduating into tech, finance or another competitive professional field. But the picture is more complicated than “AI has taken the graduate jobs.” The Institute of Student Employers’ 2026 research found that 87% of employers expect AI to reshape graduate and apprentice roles over the next three years. Importantly, employers generally expect roles to be changed rather than simply replaced. And new Skills England research published in October shows that demand still exists in important areas: software development, IT business analysis and several engineering occupations appear repeatedly as priority skills across UK growth sectors. In digital and technology, around 68% of priority occupations are considered to be in critical or elevated demand, while the equivalent figure in financial services is around 70%. So what is changing? Employers increasingly want graduates who can work beyond routine tasks. In tech, AI is shifting value towards verification, judgement and communication; in finance, it is transforming analytics, fraud detection and risk; and engineering demand remains strong across areas such as clean energy, advanced manufacturing and defence. The goal is not simply to become an “AI expert” — it is to combine your profession with practical AI literacy and strong human judgement. For international graduates, this matters even more because sponsorship adds another filter to an already competitive market. Your application needs to show what you can contribute, not just that you have a degree and need sponsorship. Whether you are in finance, software or engineering, combine your technical skills with data, AI literacy, problem-solving and communication. And remember: a government “priority occupation” is not automatically sponsorable immigration eligibility still needs to be checked separately. My takeaway for graduates entering the 2026/27 market is simple: don’t try to compete with AI at the repetitive tasks it can increasingly perform. Build the skills that make you valuable alongside it judgement, verification, problem-solving, technical depth, communication and the ability to apply technology to real business problems. Sources: Skills England Annual Skills Report and Sector Skills Needs Assessments 2026 #GraduateJobs #InternationalGraduates #InternationalStudents #EngineeringJobs #FinanceCareers #TechCareers #ArtificialIntelligence #VisaSponsorship #UKJobs #GraduateCareers

posts.headline: Experienced technologist. AI Pragmatist | Web3 | E-Commerce | Angel Investor
posts.text: Last month, 24th August. I was on a panel at DevOps Summit Singapore. And the topic: the socio-technical architecture of software-enabled organisations. The point I kept coming back to was this. With AI writing more of the code, the engineer's job moves to specification, verification and orchestration, a point that my fellow panelist Abhik Roychoudhury mentioned when he said that verification and validation is now more important than ever. In my team at Mighty Jaxx, that is already how we work, from using MCP servers for Figma to Shopify code to QA agents. But the code was never the hard part. Someone still has to say exactly what we want, and check that what comes back is correct. That also raises a question which I care about: where do junior engineers learn if AI takes the entry-level tasks? I don't have a full answer yet. But hiring, mentoring and giving interns real work is a good place to start. And interns are expected to be given knottier problems to solve much sooner and the acceleration along the learning curve will accelerate. Now is in fact, a great time to be a software developer as demand will outpace supply It was a session of good questions and great conversations. Thanks to everyone who came by to chat after the session. And thanks to my panel host Sergiu Bodiu and my fellow panelists Albert Xu Ray Booysen and Abhik Roychoudhury for a great discussion. #DevOpsSummitSG #DevOps #AI #EngineeringLeadership

posts.headline: Senior Backend Engineer | Python, Node.js, Laravel | SaaS, AI Integration & Agents
posts.text: Companies are opening more roles, not fewer. If AI were replacing engineers, hiring activity would be dropping, but the demand for developer talent remains active. If anyone can build software with AI, what exactly are companies hiring developers for? AI makes writing code fast, letting teams spin up basic templates and small features in seconds. But writing more code does not equal a working system. When teams rely on AI to write code without careful checking, they get stuck with messy code, hidden bugs, and serious security risks. This is why companies keep hiring developers. They are not looking for someone to type out basic code—AI already does that. They need engineers who understand how different systems connect, how to keep data secure, and how to fix complex problems when things break down. Writing code is cheap now. Good engineering judgment is what companies are actually paying for. #SoftwareEngineering #AI #TechHiring #BackendDevelopment #TechLeadership

posts.text: Why you should learn the full robotics software stack, not just one tool Are you an entry-level Robotics Software Engineer, or a student who has built a few robot projects? Here is a hard truth. Most robots that work in a demo fail in the real world. The reason is rarely the hardware. It is the software around it. Recruiters hiring for robotics roles in 2026 look for people who understand how the pieces connect. Here is what that stack looks like, and why each layer matters: 🔹 ROS 2: The backbone of modern robots. Nodes, topics, services and launch files are how real robot systems talk to each other. If you know ROS 2 well, you can join almost any robotics team. 🔹 Simulation (Gazebo, Isaac Sim): Test before you break hardware. A digital twin lets you stream LiDAR, cameras and IMU data and try out ideas safely. It is also where most industry testing happens now. 🔹 State estimation and perception: Sensors are noisy. Fusing them into one reliable pose, and turning a camera feed into a target, is what separates a toy from a robot you can trust. 🔹 SLAM and Navigation (Nav2): Mapping a space, planning a route and avoiding people and obstacles. This is core to warehouse, logistics and service robotics. 🔹 Manipulation (MoveIt 2): Motion planning for robot arms. Locate, pick, deliver. This is where many Physical AI jobs are heading. 🔹 Testing and failure analysis: The skill nobody teaches. Real engineers inject faults on purpose (sensor dropout, blocked paths, slipped grasps), measure what breaks, and fix it with evidence. Tracking error, latency, localisation drift, mission success rate. Numbers, not opinions. 💡 The takeaway: Do not learn these as separate tutorials. Build one robot and keep adding to it, layer by layer, until it runs a full autonomous mission. That is the project that gets you hired. 🎓 This is how we built the Quanskill Robotics Systems Level 2 course. It is 12 weeks online, one robot with a new skill every week, and strong graduates move on to a 3-month internship with QuanRobotics. The first batch starts in November, and each batch has only 10 seats. The application link is in the comments. 📚 References: ROS 2: docs.ros.org Gazebo: gazebosim.org Nav2: nav2.org MoveIt 2: moveit.ros.org Isaac Sim: https://lnkd.in/gSm6qef7 Which layer of the stack do you find hardest? posts.text: 1,000 junior tech jobs are never publicly posted. That's right. Many entry-level roles get filled through direct connections, referrals, or before they even hit major job boards. For new grads, interns, and career changers, this means you need to go beyond just applying online. You need to find the people who are actually hiring. Here's a LinkedIn search hack to uncover these hidden opportunities and connect with the right decision-makers: 1. Go to LinkedIn's main search bar. 2. Type your desired role (e.g., "Junior Software Engineer"). 3. Click on the "People" filter, then "All filters." 4. Now, for your secret weapon filters: a. "Title": Add terms like "Engineering Manager," "Director of Engineering," "Hiring Manager," "Head of Talent." b. "Current Company": Input specific companies you want to work for. c. "Location": Target your desired cities or regions. d. "Industry": Narrow down to "Computer Software," "Information Technology," etc. 5. Hit "Show results." You'll now see profiles of people directly responsible for building tech teams. Look at their "Posts" section for direct hiring announcements. Check their "About" section for interests or open roles. Send a personalized connection request. Reference something specific from their profile or a company project. This isn't just about finding a job; it's about building relationships that lead to your first tech opportunity. HireMe helps you find junior roles. This helps you get noticed by the right people. posts.text: 1969. Houston, United States. A team of scientists and engineers is preparing a mission that will take human beings to the Moon. Among them is a remarkable woman: Margaret Hamilton, Director of the Software Engineering Division for the Apollo programme. At the time, software engineering is still an emerging discipline. Yet Hamilton understands something fundamental: The success of a complex project does not depend on one individual, but on the ability to bring different areas of expertise together. She champions rigour, anticipates potential failures and insists on preparing for the unexpected. During the Apollo 11 mission, computer overload alarms threaten the lunar landing. But the software has been designed to prioritise critical tasks, allowing the crew to continue their mission. This achievement is no stroke of luck. It is the result of collective effort, clear vision and trust in the expertise of others. Her story offers a powerful management lesson: You can lead a complex project without being the person who knows every technical detail. Even today, some managers believe they must be the most competent person on their team. What a mistake! Hiring someone more talented than you is not a threat. Listening to your colleagues is not a sign of weakness. Surrounding yourself with strong personalities does not diminish your authority. Acknowledging your limitations does not undermine your leadership. A mediocre manager wants to be the smartest person in the room. A great manager wants to bring the smartest minds around the table. Shine on ✨

posts.text: Recruitment is bigger than just hiring people! 🎯 Here are 30 types of recruiters every HR professional should know, explained in the simplest words. 🔹 Technical Recruiter — Hires people for technical roles. 🔹 IT Recruiter — Hires software developers, IT engineers, and tech professionals. 🔹 Non-Technical Recruiter — Hires for non-technical roles like HR, sales, and operations. 🔹 Finance Recruiter — Hires accountants, financial analysts, and finance professionals. 🔹 Sales Recruiter — Hires sales executives, managers, and sales leaders. 🔹 Marketing Recruiter — Hires marketers, brand managers, and digital marketing professionals. 🔹 HR Recruiter — Hires HR professionals for different HR roles. 🔹 Healthcare Recruiter — Hires doctors, nurses, and healthcare professionals. 🔹 Engineering Recruiter — Hires engineers across different engineering fields. 🔹 Executive Recruiter — Hires senior leaders and top-level executives. 🔹 Entry-Level Recruiter — Hires freshers, interns, and junior employees. 🔹 Mid-Level Recruiter — Hires experienced professionals and managers. 🔹 Senior-Level Recruiter — Hires senior managers, directors, and department heads. 🔹 Executive Search Recruiter — Finds top executives for critical leadership positions. 🔹 Campus Recruiter — Hires students and fresh graduates from colleges. 🔹 Blue-Collar Recruiter — Hires workers for factories, warehouses, and field jobs. 🔹 Full-Cycle Recruiter — Manages the hiring process from job opening to offer. 🔹 Recruitment Sourcer — Finds potential candidates for open positions. 🔹 Recruitment Coordinator — Schedules interviews and manages hiring logistics. 🔹 Recruitment Operations Specialist — Manages recruitment systems, processes, and reports. 🔹 Recruitment Analyst — Uses recruitment data to identify trends and improve hiring. 🔹 Employer Branding Specialist — Makes a company attractive to potential employees. 🔹 In-House Recruiter — Hires employees directly for their own company. 🔹 Agency Recruiter — Hires candidates for client companies through an agency. 🔹 Contract Recruiter — Supports hiring for a fixed period or specific project. 🔹 RPO Recruiter — Recruits for a company through an outsourced recruitment team. 🔹 Freelance Recruiter — Works independently to find and hire candidates. 🔹 Global Recruiter — Hires candidates across different countries. 🔹 Talent Intelligence Specialist — Studies talent markets to understand where the right candidates can be found. 🔹 Talent Acquisition Partner — Works with business leaders to plan hiring and meet talent needs. Remember: Recruitment is not just about filling vacancies. It is about finding the right talent to help businesses grow. 👇 Which type of recruiter are you? #HumanResources #Recruitment #TalentAcquisition #HRProfessionals #CareerGrowth

posts.text: 𝗔𝗜 𝗶𝘀 𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗵𝗼𝘄 𝘄𝗲 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱 𝘀𝗼𝗳𝘁𝘄𝗮𝗿𝗲. 𝗕𝘂𝘁 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝘄𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮𝗯𝗼𝘂𝘁 𝘄𝗵𝗼 𝘄𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗯𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱 𝗶𝘁 𝘁𝗼𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗿𝗼𝘄? Recently, I had the opportunity to attend Walmart’s flagship tech conference, 𝗖𝗼𝗻𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗴𝗲, and listen to inspiring speakers discuss AI adoption, its impact, future possibilities, and the risks that come with its rapid growth. One thought stayed with me. As organisations race to adopt AI, improve productivity, and build leaner teams, are we overlooking the future of fresh talent? AI can now write code, generate tests, and speed up development. Experienced engineers are increasingly focusing on architecture, reviewing AI-generated code, and making complex technical decisions. A few facts worth reflecting on: • Stanford research: Employment among software developers aged 22–25 declined nearly 20% from its late-2022 peak through 2025, according to research on early-career employment and AI exposure. • Gartner (2026): Its survey found that some organisations have stopped hiring for certain entry-level roles because of AI automation. • Industry shift: As AI takes on more routine coding and testing, the expectations from engineers are changing towards broader ownership, system design, and technical judgement. These trends raise an important question. If fresh graduates get fewer opportunities to learn by doing, where will tomorrow’s experienced engineers come from? Engineering judgement, architecture, and problem-solving don’t develop overnight. They come from hands-on experience, learning from mistakes, and mentorship. The answer isn’t to slow down AI adoption. It’s to rethink how we develop talent alongside it — helping fresh graduates learn to build with AI, not simply expecting AI to replace the learning process. posts.text: Ever since I moved to Melbourne and started living independently, I've wanted to be frugal and cook more at home. But I never knew what to make that was both nutritious and actually tasty. If you're a uni student or fresh grad, you've probably been there too. So I decided to do something about it. posts.text: Software agencies died in 2026. That’s what the internet keeps telling us. So I went through the arguments. Take 1: No. AI hasn’t killed agencies. It changed what developers do. Take 2: No. AI lets people solve problems faster without paying developers, designers and agencies a fortune. Take 3: Yes. Why hire five people when one person with AI can do the work? Take 4: Hell no. A ChatGPT employee says AI is trying to take over the world, so we’re all doomed anyway. Funny. But the job market tells a less funny story. The numbers: US software developer job postings fell 73% from their February 2022 peak to February 2025, according to Indeed data cited by Investopedia. They’ve rebounded since but are still below pre-pandemic levels. The World Economic Forum projects 92 million jobs displaced globally by 2030 and 170 million created. That covers the whole economy, not just AI. Juniors have it worst. AI handles more coding tasks, but companies still need experienced engineers to make architectural decisions, review code and solve hard problems. Entry-level roles are under pressure while senior demand shows signs of recovery. AI doesn’t need to replace every developer to disrupt the industry. It only needs to let a company do the same work with fewer people. A project that needed six people might now need three who use AI well. A client who used to hire an agency might build an MVP with one AI-savvy founder. A small agency that competed on cheap development might have nothing left to compete on. Jobs rarely disappear with an announcement. Companies just stop hiring for them. So are software agencies finished? No. But agencies that sell code as their main value have a serious problem. The ones that last will understand the client’s business problem, build reliable systems, own the outcome and use AI to deliver more with less. The others may not notice until the pipeline dries up. How much of today’s work will still need a human tomorrow? For agencies, we’re already finding out. I have a strong case study but have got no more energy to write, good night!
